newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel says devaluation no basis for growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel says devaluation no basis for growth.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday lashed back at a pointed French attack on the monetary policies of the German central bank, laying down the law that Germany would not sanction devaluation strategies for growth.

"Growth and employment cannot be reached through a targeted exchange rate policy," Waigel told the German parliament. "Exchange rates are ultimately decided by markets on the basis of economic fundamentals.

"Favourable fundamental data are created above all by credible, stability-oriented monetary, economic and financial policies...I reject the criticism of the policy of the Bundesbank, within Germany and without."

Waigel's comments came the day after a Bank of France council member attacked the Bundesbank for lack of understanding on monetary and exchange rate policy, saying this was damaging Europe's single currency plans.

Expressing a minority view within the Bank of France, council member Jean-Pierre Gerard said the only way to counter this could lie in devaluing the French franc, which would force the future single currency, the euro, down to a weaker rate against world currencies.
Such policies are anathema to the Germans, who have built up their postwar economy on the premise that a stable currency is the prerequisite for economic growth.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl restated this in parliament this week. "We want a hard currency and don't want to get into a weak currency situation," he said. "That is not arrogance, but comes from our experience in Germany over the past 50 years."
With the damage of two bouts of hyperinflation etched into the national psyche, the German public is extremely weary of exchanging the cherished marks for an unproven euro.
The Bundesbank, expressly charged with the task of maintaining the value of the mark, is also determined the new euro will be a hard currency as soon as it is launched in 1999.

But German analysts said even strong assurances from French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, who made clear Gerard's view was not the official Paris view, were not enough to calm their concern about France's stance.

"German officials were already a bit worried by the lack of French concern over issues such as France Telecom in their budget," Thomas Mayer, chief economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, said of the use of part of a France Telecom's pension fund to reduce France's budget deficit.
Reassurances that Paris was not in favour of a devaluation strategy were simply not enough to contain these worries, given the unpopular position of the French government, Mayer added.

"If you look at the French government they seem to be pretty much beleaguered," he said. "They are having to defend themselves against an onslaught from all sides -- the truckers, industrialists who want a weaker franc and some politicians".
Eckhard Schulte, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan, also said he believed the dispute stemmed from a deep-rooted clash of ideologies between France and Germany.

"It is becoming more and more evident that there are basic differences between the two sides and that these are growing more pronounced as the 1999 deadline nears," he said of the target for introducing the single currency.
Economists said that any persistent difference of opinion with France could present Germany with strong opposition on its current number one priority -- a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline.

Agreement on the terms of the pact has so far been elusive, with Germany seemingly almost alone in seeking the strictest possible terms for the pact. Many others believe job creation must sometimes be a higher goal than spending cutbacks.
In his speech, Waigel warned that those in Europe who considered a stability pact less important than a pact for jobs were "embarking on a dangerous path".

But Schulte argued that Germany may have to drop some of its demands for the terms of the pact if it is to get a deal at all. "Germany has often proved strongest in the past, but this time it may have to back down and seek a compromise," he said.
